A Tutorial on funcml: A Functional Machine Learning Framework for R

Author

Imad El Badisy

Published

May 13, 2026

Abstract

Machine learning workflows in R are frequently fragmented across incompatible packages and object systems, creating cognitive overhead for both researchers and practitioners. The funcml package addresses this fragmentation by providing a deliberate, formula-first framework that unifies supervised learning, resampling-based evaluation, hyperparameter tuning, learner comparison, model-agnostic interpretation, and plug-in causal estimation through six top-level verbs: fit(), evaluate(), tune(), compare_learners(), interpret(), and estimate(). This tutorial provides a comprehensive, self-contained introduction to funcml with emphasis on the statistical theory and algorithmic foundations underlying each component. For every learner in the registry—spanning generalized linear models, regularized regression, tree-based methods, ensemble methods, support vector machines, neural networks, additive models, Bayesian trees, discriminant analysis, and ensemble aggregation—we present the governing equations, key assumptions, and hyperparameter landscape, followed by reproducible R code. We cover all fourteen model-agnostic interpretability methods with theoretical motivation and worked examples, and conclude with plug-in g-computation for average and conditional treatment-effect estimation. The tutorial is designed to be read progressively, with each section building on the preceding one.

Keywords

R package, machine learning, model interpretation, explainable AI, resampling, hyperparameter tuning, g-computation, tutorial

1 Introduction

Supervised machine learning comprises a collection of algorithms that map feature matrices to responses: estimating a function \(\hat{f}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) (regression) or \(\hat{f}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \{1,\ldots,K\}\) (classification) that generalises well to new data (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009). Applied workflows inevitably involve more than a single fit-and-predict call. Practitioners need resampling-based performance estimation, hyperparameter search, multi-learner benchmarks, post-hoc interpretation, and increasingly links between predictive models and causal questions.

In R, these tasks are scattered across multiple frameworks. caret (Kuhn 2008) standardised model fitting and resampling under one interface but has largely been superseded. mlr3 (Lang et al. 2019) provides a powerful object-oriented system based on R6 with a rich ecosystem of extensions. tidymodels (Kuhn and Wickham 2019) integrates with the tidyverse and offers deep preprocessing support. iml (Molnar, Casalicchio, and Bischl 2018) unifies model-agnostic interpretation. Each of these is excellent within its design space, but combining them across a single analysis requires navigating incompatible object systems and learning several different programming paradigms.

The funcml package (Badisy 2026) was built for a different point in the design space: a compact, formula-first framework that keeps machine learning close to native R modeling conventions while supporting the full applied workflow through a small number of stable verbs.

NoteDesign philosophy

funcml is intentionally opinionated. Preprocessing—imputation, encoding, scaling—is expected to happen before any funcml call. The package provides modeling, not pipeline orchestration. This keeps the API surface small and function arguments transparent: every input to fit() or evaluate() is visible in the call.

The interface revolves around six verbs (Table 1), each returning a stable S3 object with consistent print(), summary(), and plot() methods.

This tutorial walks through each verb in order. Section 2 covers installation and introduces the running datasets. Section 3 gives a visual overview of the complete pipeline. Section 4 introduces resampling generators, which underpin evaluation, tuning, and comparison. Section 5 presents all 23 learners with statistical foundations and R code. Section 6 covers the metric library. Section 7 through Section 9 demonstrate evaluation, tuning, and benchmarking. Section 10 covers all fourteen interpretation methods. Section 11 presents g-computation for causal effect estimation. Section 12 ties everything together in a single end-to-end example.

Notation. Throughout, \(n\) denotes sample size; \(p\) the number of features; \(\mathbf{x}_i = (x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{ip})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^p\) the feature vector of observation \(i\); and \(y_i\) the scalar response. \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) denotes the full feature matrix and \(\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) the response vector. \(\hat{f}\) always refers to the estimated prediction function.

2 Installation and Datasets

2.1 Installation

funcml is available from GitHub and can be installed with:

remotes::install_github("ielbadisy/funcml")
library(funcml)

2.2 Datasets

funcml ships with fifteen curated datasets covering regression, binary classification, and multiclass classification. The full list can be inspected at any time:

data(package = "funcml")

Throughout this tutorial we use three representative datasets that together cover the three main supervised learning tasks.

Birthweight (regression). The birthweight dataset (Hosmer and Lemeshow 1989) contains 189 mother–infant pairs. The outcome is birth weight in grams (birth_weight_g); predictors include maternal age, pre-pregnancy weight, race, smoking status, and obstetric history.

data_reg   <- birthweight
formula_reg <- birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
dim(data_reg)
#> [1] 189  10

Pima Diabetes (binary classification). The pimadiabetes dataset (Smith et al. 1988) contains 532 patients from the Pima Indian Diabetes Database. The outcome is a diabetes diagnosis indicator (diabetes; "Yes" / "No"). We use the pre-specified training partition and discard the split indicator.1

data_cls   <- pimadiabetes[pimadiabetes$split == "train", ]
data_cls   <- data_cls[, setdiff(names(data_cls), "split")]
formula_cls <- diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
dim(data_cls)
#> [1] 200   8
table(data_cls$diabetes)
#> 
#>  No Yes 
#> 132  68

Thyroid Function (multiclass). The newthyroid dataset contains 215 patients classified as normal (1), hyperthyroid (2), or hypothyroid (3) based on five thyroid laboratory measurements.

data_mc   <- newthyroid
data_mc$class <- factor(data_mc$class)
formula_mc <- class ~ t3_resin_uptake + total_serum_thyroxin +
  total_serum_triiodothyronine + basal_tsh + max_abs_tsh_diff
dim(data_mc)
#> [1] 215   6
table(data_mc$class)
#> 
#>   1   2   3 
#> 150  35  30

With the package loaded and data prepared, we next describe how these pieces fit together into a coherent analysis pipeline.

3 The funcml Workflow

The funcml pipeline flows from raw data through a fitted model to performance assessment, interpretation, and causal estimation. Each stage corresponds to one of the six top-level verbs introduced in Section 1.

The package follows a preprocessing-outside design: data passed to any funcml verb is exactly the data that will be modelled. There are no hidden transformations, no formula preprocessing pipelines, and no implicit encoding steps. This transparency is deliberate — it keeps the function arguments self-documenting and avoids hidden state that can cause silent errors between training and prediction.2

The learner registry and all available metrics and interpretation methods can be queried at runtime, making the package self-documenting:

list_learners() |> head(8)
#>      learner   fit   predict   tune has_fit has_predict has_tune available
#> 15  adaboost fit() predict() tune()    TRUE        TRUE     TRUE      TRUE
#> 22      bart fit() predict() tune()    TRUE        TRUE     TRUE      TRUE
#> 9        C50 fit() predict() tune()    TRUE        TRUE     TRUE      TRUE
#> 18   cforest fit() predict() tune()    TRUE        TRUE     TRUE      TRUE
#> 17     ctree fit() predict() tune()    TRUE        TRUE     TRUE      TRUE
#> 6  e1071_svm fit() predict() tune()    TRUE        TRUE     TRUE      TRUE
#> 11     earth fit() predict() tune()    TRUE        TRUE     TRUE      TRUE
#> 14       fda fit() predict() tune()    TRUE        TRUE     TRUE      TRUE
list_metrics() |> head(8)
#>      metric direction
#> 1      rmse  minimize
#> 2       mae  minimize
#> 3       mse  minimize
#> 4     medae  minimize
#> 5      mape  minimize
#> 6       rsq  maximize

The first concrete design choice in any analysis is how to partition the data for honest performance estimation. That is where the tutorial begins.

4 Resampling Strategies

4.1 Theory

Performance on training data is an optimistic estimate of generalisation performance because the model has already seen the training observations. The standard remedy is to hold out data during training, evaluate on the held-out portion, and repeat in a systematic way. Formally, given a dataset \(\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), the goal is to estimate the expected prediction error:

\[ \text{Err} = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, y),\, \mathcal{D}} \bigl[L\!\bigl(y,\, \hat{f}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)\bigr] \]

where \(L\) is a loss function and \(\hat{f}_{\mathcal{D}}\) is the model trained on \(\mathcal{D}\) (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009).

\(K\)-fold cross-validation (Stone 1974) partitions \(\mathcal{D}\) into \(K\) folds of roughly equal size. The model is trained on \(K-1\) folds and evaluated on the held-out fold, rotating until every observation has served as a validation observation exactly once:

\[ \widehat{\text{CV}}(K) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n L\!\bigl(y_i,\, \hat{f}^{-\kappa(i)}(\mathbf{x}_i)\bigr) \]

where \(\kappa(i)\) maps observation \(i\) to its fold and \(\hat{f}^{-\kappa(i)}\) is the model trained on all folds except \(\kappa(i)\). Setting \(K = n\) gives leave-one-out CV (LOO-CV).3 Common choices are \(K = 5\) and \(K = 10\).

Holdout validation reserves a fixed fraction \(\pi \in (0, 1)\) of observations for testing. While computationally cheap, it is high-variance: performance depends heavily on the particular random split, especially when \(n\) is small.

Grouped cross-validation ensures that observations sharing a group identifier — patients, hospitals, geographic clusters — are never split across folds. Without this constraint, leakage between correlated observations produces optimistic estimates.

Time-series cross-validation respects the temporal order of observations by expanding or rolling the training window. Fold \(k\) trains on \(\{1, \ldots, t_k\}\) and evaluates on \(\{t_k+1, \ldots, t_k+h\}\) for an assessment horizon \(h\), preventing future data from informing past predictions.

4.2 funcml Resampling Constructors

All four strategies are created with dedicated constructors that return objects accepted by evaluate(), tune(), and compare_learners() without modification:

cv5   <- cv(v = 5, seed = 42)              # 5-fold CV
cv5r  <- cv(v = 5, repeats = 3, seed = 42) # repeated CV
ho    <- holdout(prop = 0.8, seed = 42)    # 80/20 holdout
# group_cv(v = 5, group = "patient_id")   # grouped CV
# time_cv(initial = 50, assess = 10)      # time-series CV
TipChoosing a resampling strategy

Use 5-fold CV as the default. Increase to 10 folds when \(n < 200\). Use repeated CV when you need low-variance estimates of confidence intervals. Use grouped CV whenever observations within a group are correlated (e.g., repeat measurements, clustered designs). Use holdout only when \(n\) is large enough that a single split is stable (roughly \(n > 2000\)).

With a resampling strategy in hand, we can now explore the learners available in the registry.

5 The Learner Registry

5.1 Overview

The funcml registry contains 23 learners spanning ten algorithmic families (Table 2). All are accessed through a string identifier passed to model =. The registry is queryable and extensible: list_learners() returns a data frame of all learners with columns for task compatibility, probability output, multiclass support, native feature importance, and tunable hyperparameters.

NoteThe bias–variance tradeoff

Every learner navigates a fundamental tradeoff. Bias is the systematic error from an overly simple model (underfitting). Variance is the sensitivity of predictions to fluctuations in the training set (overfitting). The expected prediction error decomposes as: \[ \mathbb{E}\!\left[(y - \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}))^2\right] = \text{Bias}^2(\hat{f}) + \text{Var}(\hat{f}) + \sigma^2 \] where \(\sigma^2\) is irreducible noise. Simple models (GLM, single tree) have high bias and low variance. Complex models (deep forests, boosting with many rounds) have low bias but high variance. Regularisation, pruning, and ensembling are strategies for controlling this tradeoff. Hyperparameter tuning (Section 8) navigates the tradeoff empirically by selecting the configuration with the best cross-validated error.

5.2 Linear Models

Linear models are the natural starting point: they are interpretable, computationally cheap, and well-understood statistically. Their coefficients are directly interpretable as marginal effects (on the link scale), and they provide baselines against which more complex learners should be compared.

5.2.1 Generalised Linear Models (glm)

Theory. A generalised linear model (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009) links a conditional mean \(\mu_i = \mathbb{E}[y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i]\) to a linear predictor \(\eta_i\) through a monotone differentiable link function \(g\):

\[ g(\mu_i) = \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} = \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\beta} \]

The response is assumed to follow an exponential family distribution. The three most common specifications are:

Task Distribution Link \(g\) \(g(\mu)\)
Regression Gaussian Identity \(\mu\)
Binary classification Binomial Logit \(\log\tfrac{\mu}{1-\mu}\)
Count regression Poisson Log \(\log\mu\)

Parameters \(\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^{p+1}\) are estimated by maximum likelihood via iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS).4 In funcml, the GLM uses family = "gaussian" for regression and family = "binomial" for classification automatically based on the response type.

fit_glm_reg <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "glm")
fit_glm_reg
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: glm
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189
fit_glm_cls <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "glm")
predict(fit_glm_cls, newdata = data_cls[1:3, ], type = "prob")
#>          No        Yes
#> 1 0.9368186 0.06318139
#> 2 0.1860615 0.81393846
#> 3 0.9265270 0.07347296

5.2.2 Elastic Net Regularisation (glmnet)

Theory. Ordinary least squares overfits when \(p\) is large or when predictors are correlated. The elastic net (Zou and Hastie 2005) adds a combined \(\ell_1\)/\(\ell_2\) penalty to the loss:

\[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\left\{ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n L(y_i, \eta_i) + \lambda\!\left[(1-\alpha)\frac{\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2}{2} + \alpha\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_1\right] \right\} \]

The mixing parameter \(\alpha \in [0, 1]\) controls the blend between ridge (\(\alpha = 0\)) and lasso (\(\alpha = 1\)) (Tibshirani 1996; J. Friedman, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2010). The \(\ell_2\) component handles correlated predictors gracefully — ridge regression distributes coefficients across a correlated group rather than arbitrarily zeroing some. The \(\ell_1\) component induces sparsity — some coefficients are shrunk exactly to zero, performing variable selection. The intermediate elastic net inherits both properties.5 The regularisation path over \(\lambda\) is computed efficiently by coordinate descent (J. Friedman, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2010).

Key hyperparameters: alpha (mixing, default 1 = lasso), lambda (shrinkage strength; cross-validated internally by default).

fit_glmnet <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "glmnet",
                  spec = list(alpha = 0.5))
fit_glmnet
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: glmnet
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.2.3 Partial Least Squares (pls)

Theory. When \(p > n\) or when predictors are highly collinear, even ridge regression may struggle. Partial least squares (Wold 1975; Mevik and Wehrens 2007) extracts a small number of latent components that simultaneously maximise the covariance between \(\mathbf{X}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\). The \(k\)-th component direction \(\mathbf{w}_k\) solves:

\[ \mathbf{w}_k, \mathbf{q}_k = \arg\max_{\|\mathbf{w}\|=\|\mathbf{q}\|=1} \operatorname{Cov}^2(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w},\, \mathbf{y}\mathbf{q}) \]

subject to orthogonality with previous directions (NIPALS algorithm). Unlike principal component regression (PCR), which finds directions of maximum variance in \(\mathbf{X}\) irrespective of \(\mathbf{y}\), PLS finds directions that are most predictive of the response.

Key hyperparameter: ncomp (number of latent components; typically selected by CV).

fit_pls <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "pls",
               spec = list(ncomp = 3))
fit_pls
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: pls
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.3 Decision Trees

Decision trees trade interpretability for flexibility: each split corresponds to an if-then rule that can be stated in plain language. Single trees, however, have high variance — small changes in training data can produce very different tree structures. The ensemble methods in Section 5.4 and Section 5.5 address this limitation.

5.3.1 CART Decision Trees (rpart)

Theory. Classification and regression trees (CART) (Breiman et al. 1984) recursively partition \(\mathbb{R}^p\) into hyper-rectangular regions. At each node, the algorithm finds the feature \(j\) and split point \(s\) that minimise the weighted impurity of the two child nodes:

\[ (j^*, s^*) = \arg\min_{j,\, s} \left[ \min_{c_L} \sum_{i:\, x_{ij} \le s} L(y_i, c_L) + \min_{c_R} \sum_{i:\, x_{ij} > s} L(y_i, c_R) \right] \]

For regression, \(L(y, c) = (y - c)^2\) and the optimal leaf constant is the within-leaf mean. For classification, the most common split criteria are:

Gini impurity — measures the probability that a randomly chosen observation is misclassified if its label is drawn from the leaf distribution: \[ \text{Gini}(p_1, \ldots, p_K) = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^K p_k^2 \]

Cross-entropy (deviance) — the information-theoretic entropy of the leaf distribution: \[ H(p_1, \ldots, p_K) = -\sum_{k=1}^K p_k \log p_k \]

Both criteria reach zero for a pure leaf (\(p_k = 1\) for some \(k\)) and are maximised for a uniform distribution. The tree is grown until a stopping criterion is met (minimum node size or maximum depth), then pruned by minimising the cost-complexity objective: \[ R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha |T| \] where \(R(T)\) is resubstitution error, \(|T|\) is the number of terminal nodes, and \(\alpha \ge 0\) is the complexity parameter.6

Key hyperparameters: cp (complexity, default 0.01), minsplit (minimum observations to attempt a split), maxdepth.

fit_rpart <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "rpart",
                 spec = list(cp = 0.01, minsplit = 10))
fit_rpart
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: rpart
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.3.2 Conditional Inference Trees (ctree)

Theory. Standard CART suffers from selection bias: features with more possible split points (e.g., continuous variables or factors with many levels) are more likely to be selected even if they have no true association with the response (Hothorn, Hornik, and Zeileis 2006). Conditional inference trees decouple variable selection from split determination using permutation tests.

At each node, an association test is performed for each feature \(X_j\) against the response \(Y\). The feature with the smallest Bonferroni-adjusted \(p\)-value is selected:

\[ p_j^* = P\!\left(\sup_s |T(X_j, Y, s)| > t_{\text{obs}}\right) \]

where \(T\) is an appropriate linear test statistic derived from conditional distributions. A split is performed only if \(\min_j p_j^* < \alpha_{\text{split}}\); otherwise the node becomes a leaf. This approach is unbiased toward any specific type of predictor and provides a principled stopping criterion.

Key hyperparameter: mincriterion (\(1 - \alpha_{\text{split}}\); higher values produce smaller trees).

fit_ctree <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "ctree",
                 spec = list(mincriterion = 0.95))
fit_ctree
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: ctree
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.3.3 C5.0 Decision Trees (C50)

Theory. C5.0 (Quinlan 1993) is the commercial successor to C4.5 and ID3. Instead of Gini impurity, C5.0 selects the split feature by maximising the gain ratio, which normalises information gain by the entropy of the split itself:

\[ \text{GainRatio}(X_j) = \frac{H(Y) - H(Y \mid X_j)}{H(X_j)} \]

The denominator \(H(X_j) = -\sum_v p(X_j = v)\log p(X_j = v)\) penalises features that create many small branches (e.g., a unique-ID feature would have maximum information gain but minimal gain ratio). C5.0 also natively supports boosting by sequentially fitting weighted trees.

Key hyperparameters: trials (boosting rounds; 1 = single tree), minCases (minimum observations per leaf).

fit_C50 <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "C50",
               spec = list(trials = 1))
fit_C50
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: C50
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.4 Random Forests

Single decision trees are interpretable but unstable. The two random forest variants in funcml address this by combining many trees grown on resampled versions of the data, reducing variance while preserving the low bias of individual deep trees.

5.4.1 Random Forests (ranger, randomForest)

Theory. Random forests (Breiman 2001a) combine bootstrap aggregation (bagging (Breiman 1996a)) with random subspace sampling. Given \(B\) bootstrap datasets \(\mathcal{D}^{*(b)}\), each tree \(\hat{f}^{(b)}\) is grown using only a random subset of \(m \le p\) candidate features at each node. The ensemble averages:

\[ \hat{f}_{\text{RF}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat{f}^{(b)}(\mathbf{x}) \quad (\text{regression}) \] \[ \hat{f}_{\text{RF}}(\mathbf{x}) = \arg\max_k \sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{f}^{(b)}(\mathbf{x}) = k\right] \quad (\text{classification, majority vote}) \]

Random feature sampling decorrelates the trees: if a few very strong predictors exist, every tree would otherwise split on them first, producing correlated predictions. Decorrelated trees reduce the ensemble variance without increasing individual tree bias.

The out-of-bag (OOB) error provides a free, nearly unbiased estimate of generalisation error: each observation is predicted only by trees for which it was not in the bootstrap sample (\(\approx 1/e \approx 37\%\) of trees).7

Breiman’s mean-decrease impurity (MDI) importance for feature \(j\) sums the weighted impurity reduction across all splits on \(j\) across all trees: \[ \text{MDI}(j) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}^{(b)}_j} \frac{n_t}{n}\,\Delta\text{Impurity}(t) \]

Standard default: \(m = \lfloor\sqrt{p}\rfloor\) for classification, \(m = \lfloor p/3 \rfloor\) for regression.8

Key hyperparameters: num.trees / ntree (forest size; larger is better but with diminishing returns), mtry (features per split), min.node.size.

fit_ranger <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "ranger",
                  spec = list(num.trees = 300, mtry = 3, seed = 42))
fit_ranger
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: ranger
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189
fit_rf <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "randomForest",
              spec = list(ntree = 300, mtry = 3))
fit_rf
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: randomForest
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.4.2 Conditional Forest (cforest)

Theory. Conditional forests (Strobl et al. 2007, 2008) replace the CART base learner in random forests with unbiased conditional inference trees (Section 5.2.2). Each split in each tree is selected by a permutation test rather than by impurity maximisation, preventing bias toward predictors with many categories or continuous scales.

The conditional permutation importance for feature \(j\) measures the drop in performance when \(j\) is permuted within blocks defined by other correlated features, thereby controlling for feature associations:

\[ \text{CPI}(j) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ L(y, \hat{f}(\mathbf{x})) - L(y, \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}_j^{\pi})) \right] \]

where \(\mathbf{x}_j^{\pi}\) replaces \(x_j\) with a permuted value drawn from observations with similar values of correlated features. This removes the spurious importance inflation that unconditioned permutation importance assigns to correlated predictors (Strobl et al. 2008).

fit_cforest <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "cforest",
                   spec = list(ntree = 100))
fit_cforest
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: cforest
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.5 Ensemble Methods: Boosting

Boosting builds an ensemble sequentially, with each new learner correcting the errors of the previous ensemble. This contrasts with bagging, which builds trees in parallel on independent bootstrap samples.

5.5.1 Gradient Boosting Machines (gbm)

Theory. Gradient boosting (J. H. Friedman 2001a) fits an additive model \(\hat{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{m=0}^M \nu h_m(\mathbf{x})\) by functional gradient descent. At each stage \(m\), a base learner \(h_m\) (usually a shallow decision tree) is fit to the negative gradient of the loss — the pseudo-residuals:

\[ r_{im} = -\left[\frac{\partial L(y_i, F(\mathbf{x}_i))} {\partial F(\mathbf{x}_i)} \right]_{F = \hat{F}_{m-1}} \]

For squared-error loss, the pseudo-residuals are simply the ordinary residuals \(y_i - \hat{F}_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}_i)\), so gradient boosting with MSE loss is equivalent to iterative residual fitting. For log-loss, the pseudo-residuals are \(y_i - p_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}_i)\), where \(p_{m-1}\) is the current predicted probability.

The shrinkage factor \(\nu \in (0, 1)\) (learning rate) scales each tree’s contribution. Small \(\nu\) requires more trees but often achieves better generalisation.9

Key hyperparameters: n.trees, interaction.depth (tree depth, default 1 = stumps), shrinkage (learning rate), n.minobsinnode.

fit_gbm <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "gbm",
               spec = list(n.trees = 200, interaction.depth = 3,
                           shrinkage = 0.05, n.minobsinnode = 5))
fit_gbm
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: gbm
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.5.2 Extreme Gradient Boosting (xgboost)

Theory. XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin 2016) extends gradient boosting with regularisation and an efficient second-order Taylor approximation of the loss. At iteration \(m\), the optimal tree structure \(q\) maximises:

\[ \tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{(m)}(q) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|T|} \frac{\left(\sum_{i \in I_\ell} g_i\right)^2} {\sum_{i \in I_\ell} h_i + \lambda} + \gamma |T| \]

where \(g_i = \partial_{\hat{y}} L(y_i, \hat{y})\) and \(h_i = \partial^2_{\hat{y}} L(y_i, \hat{y})\) are the first and second gradient statistics, \(I_\ell\) is the set of observations at leaf \(\ell\), \(\lambda\) controls \(\ell_2\) leaf weight regularisation, and \(\gamma\) is the minimum loss reduction required for a split. Using second-order information accelerates convergence and enables more aggressive regularisation than first-order methods. XGBoost also supports column and row subsampling.

Key hyperparameters: nrounds, max_depth, eta (learning rate), subsample, colsample_bytree, lambda, alpha.

fit_xgb <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "xgboost",
               spec = list(nrounds = 200, max_depth = 4, eta = 0.05,
                           subsample = 0.8))
fit_xgb
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: xgboost
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.5.3 LightGBM (lightgbm)

Theory. LightGBM (Ke et al. 2017) achieves high speed and memory efficiency through two algorithmic innovations beyond standard gradient boosting.

Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS) retains all observations with large gradients (informative data points) and randomly downsamples those with small gradients. The missing gradient mass is compensated by a factor \((1-a)/b\) during histogram construction, where \(a\) is the top-gradient fraction retained and \(b\) the fraction sampled from the low-gradient group.

Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB) identifies mutually exclusive sparse features — features that are rarely non-zero simultaneously — and bundles them into a single dense feature. This reduces the effective number of features without information loss.

Additionally, LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise (best-first) rather than level-wise: at each step it splits the leaf with the greatest loss reduction regardless of tree depth. This produces asymmetric trees that can capture complex patterns more efficiently than level-wise growth, but requires careful regularisation to avoid overfitting.10

Key hyperparameters: num_leaves, learning_rate, n_estimators, min_child_samples, feature_fraction, bagging_fraction.

fit_lgbm <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "lightgbm",
                spec = list(num_leaves = 31, learning_rate = 0.05,
                            n_estimators = 200))
fit_lgbm
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: lightgbm
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.5.4 AdaBoost (adaboost)

Theory. AdaBoost (Freund and Schapire 1997) is the foundational adaptive boosting algorithm for binary classification. It reweights training observations after each round, increasing the weight of misclassified examples so that subsequent weak learners focus on them. Let \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\). Starting from uniform weights \(w_i^{(1)} = 1/n\), each round \(m\) proceeds:

  1. Fit weak learner \(h_m\) minimising weighted error: \(\varepsilon_m = \sum_i w_i^{(m)} \mathbf{1}[h_m(\mathbf{x}_i) \neq y_i]\).

  2. Compute learner weight: \(\alpha_m = \tfrac{1}{2}\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon_m}{\varepsilon_m}\).

  3. Update and renormalise observation weights: \(w_i^{(m+1)} \propto w_i^{(m)} \exp\!\bigl(-\alpha_m y_i h_m(\mathbf{x}_i)\bigr)\).

The final classifier is \(\hat{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \text{sign}\!\bigl(\sum_m \alpha_m h_m(\mathbf{x})\bigr)\). From a loss-function perspective, AdaBoost minimises the exponential loss \(\sum_i \exp(-y_i F(\mathbf{x}_i))\) stagewise (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009).11

Key hyperparameters: iter (boosting rounds), nu (shrinkage), type ("discrete" = decision stumps, "real" = probabilistic stumps).

fit_ada <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "adaboost",
               spec = list(iter = 100, nu = 1, type = "discrete"))
fit_ada
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: adaboost
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.6 Kernel and Similarity Methods

The following two learners make predictions by comparing new observations to training data. SVMs find the most informative boundary; kNN uses nearest neighbours directly.

5.6.1 Support Vector Machines (e1071_svm)

Theory. The support vector machine (Cortes and Vapnik 1995) finds the maximum-margin separating hyperplane. For binary classification with \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\), the hard-margin SVM solves:

\[ \min_{\mathbf{w}, b}\; \tfrac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \quad \text{s.t.}\quad y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top \phi(\mathbf{x}_i) + b) \ge 1 \;\; \forall i \]

The margin \(2/\|\mathbf{w}\|\) is the width of the slab between the two class boundaries; maximising it minimises generalisation error (by structural risk minimisation). When classes are not linearly separable, slack variables \(\xi_i \ge 0\) allow margin violations at cost \(C\):

\[ \min_{\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol{\xi}}\; \tfrac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i \quad \text{s.t.}\quad y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top \phi(\mathbf{x}_i) + b) \ge 1 - \xi_i \]

The kernel trick replaces \(\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)^\top\phi(\mathbf{x}_j)\) with a kernel function \(k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)\), implicitly mapping to a high-dimensional feature space without computing the map explicitly. Common kernels:

Kernel Formula Characteristic
Linear \(\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}'\) Linear boundaries
RBF/Gaussian \(\exp(-\gamma\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\|^2)\) Localised, universal approximator
Polynomial \((\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}' + r)^d\) Global polynomial boundaries

For regression (\(\varepsilon\)-SVR), the objective is the same but the constraint requires prediction errors to be within an \(\varepsilon\)-tube.

Key hyperparameters: kernel, cost (\(C\)), gamma (RBF bandwidth), epsilon (SVR insensitive tube width).

fit_svm <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "e1071_svm",
               spec = list(kernel = "radial", cost = 1, gamma = 0.1))
fit_svm
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: e1071_svm
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.6.2 Weighted \(k\)-Nearest Neighbours (kknn)

Theory. The \(k\)-nearest-neighbours classifier (Fix and Hodges 1951; Aha, Kibler, and Albert 1991) assigns label to \(\mathbf{x}\) based on the \(k\) closest training points. Weighted kNN assigns kernel-based weights that decay with distance:

\[ \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^k w_j\, y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^k w_j}, \qquad w_j = K\!\left(\frac{d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}_{(j)})}{d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}_{(k)})}\right) \]

where \(K\) is a kernel function (e.g., Epanechnikov, triangular, optimal) and \(d\) is the Minkowski distance of order \(r\) (\(r=1\): Manhattan, \(r=2\): Euclidean). kNN has no training phase; the entire dataset is stored and queried at prediction time, making prediction cost \(O(np)\) per query in the naive implementation.

WarningkNN and the curse of dimensionality

kNN degrades rapidly as \(p\) increases: in high dimensions, all points become approximately equidistant from a query, so “nearest” neighbours are no longer genuinely similar. Feature selection, dimensionality reduction, or feature scaling can mitigate this, but kNN is generally not recommended for \(p \gtrsim 20\) without careful preprocessing.

Key hyperparameters: k, kernel (weighting function), distance (Minkowski order).

fit_kknn <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "kknn",
                spec = list(k = 7, kernel = "optimal"))
fit_kknn
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: kknn
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.7 Additive and Basis-Expansion Models

The following two learners extend GLMs by allowing non-linear effects without abandoning the additive structure that makes linear models interpretable.

5.7.1 Generalised Additive Models (gam)

Theory. Generalised additive models (Hastie and Tibshirani 1986; Wood 2017) replace the linear predictor with a sum of smooth univariate functions:

\[ g(\mu_i) = \beta_0 + f_1(x_{i1}) + f_2(x_{i2}) + \cdots + f_p(x_{ip}) \]

Each \(f_j\) is a penalised regression spline, typically a thin-plate spline. Smoothness is enforced by a roughness penalty on the second derivative: \[ J(f_j) = \int \!\bigl[f_j''(x)\bigr]^2 \,dx \]

A large penalty forces \(f_j\) toward a straight line; a small penalty allows \(f_j\) to be highly wiggly. The smoothing parameter for each term is selected automatically by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) or generalised cross-validation (GCV) (Wood 2004). GAMs retain the additive structure of GLMs — each smooth can be visualised and interpreted separately — while capturing nonlinear marginal effects.12

formula_gam <- birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt
fit_gam <- fit(formula_gam, data = data_reg, model = "gam")
fit_gam
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: gam
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt
#> Features: 2 | Obs: 189

5.7.2 Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (earth)

Theory. MARS (J. H. Friedman 1991) builds a piecewise-linear model by adaptively selecting hinge functions from a basis dictionary:

\[ \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \beta_0 + \sum_{m=1}^M \beta_m B_m(\mathbf{x}) \]

Each basis function \(B_m\) is a product of one or more hinge functions \((x_j - t)_+ = \max(0, x_j - t)\) or \((t - x_j)_+\) for knot \(t\). Products of hinge functions from different features model interactions. The algorithm proceeds in two phases:

  1. Forward pass: greedily add hinge pairs that most reduce training error, potentially modelling interactions up to degree \(d\).
  2. Backward pass: prune using the GCV criterion: \[ \text{GCV}(M) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{\bigl(1 - C(M)/n\bigr)^2} \] where \(C(M)\) is an effective-degrees-of-freedom penalty. MARS performs automatic variable selection (a feature dropped in pruning contributes zero basis functions) and discovers interactions without pre-specification.

Key hyperparameters: degree (maximum interaction order; 1 = purely additive), nprune (maximum retained terms).

fit_earth <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "earth",
                 spec = list(degree = 2, nprune = 10))
fit_earth
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: earth
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.8 Bayesian Methods

Bayesian approaches place priors on model parameters and update them with data to form a posterior distribution. The posterior predictive distribution naturally quantifies prediction uncertainty, which is valuable in clinical and scientific applications.

5.8.1 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (bart)

Theory. BART (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010) represents the unknown function as a sum of \(B\) shallow regression trees:

\[ f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{b=1}^B g(\mathbf{x};\, \mathcal{T}_b, \mathcal{M}_b) \]

where \(\mathcal{T}_b\) is the \(b\)-th tree’s structure and \(\mathcal{M}_b\) its leaf parameters. The key insight is that each tree is meant to contribute only a small, regularised portion of the overall fit. This is enforced through regularisation priors:

  • Tree structure prior: branching probability at depth \(d\) is \(\alpha(1+d)^{-\beta}\), favouring shallow trees.
  • Leaf prior: \(\mu_{b\ell} \sim N(0, \sigma_\mu^2)\) with \(\sigma_\mu = 0.5/(k\sqrt{B})\), so that the prior 95% interval for \(f(\mathbf{x})\) spans the range of \(y\).
  • Error prior: \(\sigma^2 \sim \text{Inv-}\chi^2(\nu, \lambda)\).

Posterior inference uses a Gibbs sampler (backfitting MCMC): in each sweep, each tree is updated while holding the others fixed by fitting its tree to the current partial residuals. The posterior predictive distribution provides credible intervals for predictions without bootstrap.13

Key hyperparameters: ntree (number of trees, default 200), k (leaf prior tightness), ndpost (posterior draws), nskip (burn-in draws).

fit_bart <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "bart",
                spec = list(ntree = 50, ndpost = 200, nskip = 50,
                            seed = 42))
fit_bart
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: bart
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.8.2 Naive Bayes (naivebayes)

Theory. Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ theorem under the conditional independence assumption: given the class, all features are mutually independent (Good 1960):

\[ \hat{P}(Y = k \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto \hat{P}(Y = k) \prod_{j=1}^p \hat{P}(X_j = x_j \mid Y = k) \]

The class-conditional densities \(P(X_j \mid Y = k)\) are estimated parametrically (Gaussian for continuous, multinomial or Bernoulli for discrete) or non-parametrically (kernel density). At prediction time, the posterior is computed for each class and the argmax returned.

Despite the conditional independence assumption being almost always violated in practice, Naive Bayes often achieves competitive accuracy, particularly in text classification where \(p\) is very large relative to \(n\). The independence assumption essentially acts as a strong regulariser.

Key hyperparameters: usekernel (kernel density estimation for continuous features), laplace (additive/Laplace smoothing for discrete features).

fit_nb <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "naivebayes")
fit_nb
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: naivebayes
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.9 Discriminant Analysis

Discriminant analysis methods assume multivariate Gaussian class-conditional distributions and derive Bayes-optimal classification rules under those assumptions.

5.9.1 Linear Discriminant Analysis (lda)

Theory. Fisher’s linear discriminant analysis (R. A. Fisher 1936) seeks a linear projection \(\mathbf{w}\) that maximises between-class scatter relative to within-class scatter — a signal-to-noise ratio in projected space:

\[ \mathbf{w}^* = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \frac{\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{S}_B \mathbf{w}} {\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{S}_W \mathbf{w}} \]

where \(\mathbf{S}_B = \sum_k n_k (\boldsymbol{\mu}_k - \boldsymbol{\mu}) (\boldsymbol{\mu}_k - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\) is the between-class scatter matrix and \(\mathbf{S}_W = \sum_k \sum_{i: y_i = k} (\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k) (\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^\top\) the within-class scatter matrix. The solution is the leading eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}_W^{-1}\mathbf{S}_B\) (at most \(K-1\) non-zero eigenvalues).14

Under multivariate Gaussianity with a common covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), LDA is the Bayes-optimal classifier and its decision boundaries are linear hyperplanes: \[ \delta_k(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\mu}_k - \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\mu}_k + \log \pi_k \]

fit_lda <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "lda")
fit_lda
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: lda
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.9.2 Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (qda)

Theory. QDA relaxes LDA’s equal-covariance assumption. Each class has its own covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\), giving quadratic decision boundaries (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009):

\[ \delta_k(\mathbf{x}) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\log|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k| -\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k) + \log \pi_k \]

QDA requires estimating \(p(p+1)/2\) parameters per class and is only applicable when \(n_k > p\) for each class. When \(p\) is large relative to sample size, LDA — which pools the covariance estimate — typically generalises better.

fit_qda <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "qda")
fit_qda
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: qda
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.9.3 Flexible Discriminant Analysis (fda)

Theory. Flexible DA (Hastie and Tibshirani 1996) generalises LDA by replacing the linear regression step with an arbitrary smooth regression. The key insight is that LDA can be reframed as a linear regression of optimal scoring responses; FDA substitutes any regression method for the linear regression in this dual formulation. Let \(\Theta \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times (K-1)}\) be optimal scoring coefficients and \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\) a flexible regression; FDA solves:

\[ \min_{\Theta,\, \eta} \sum_{i=1}^n \|\Theta^\top \mathbf{z}_i - \eta(\mathbf{x}_i)\|^2 \quad\text{subject to orthogonality constraints} \]

where \(\mathbf{z}_i\) is the indicator-coded class vector. Substituting MARS for \(\eta\) gives FDA-MARS: non-linear decision boundaries with automatic variable selection, applicable to multiclass problems.

fit_fda <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "fda")
fit_fda
#> <funcml_fit> classification model: fda
#> Formula: diabetes ~ npreg + glu + bp + skin + bmi + ped + age
#> Features: 7 | Obs: 200

5.10 Neural Networks

5.10.1 Single-Hidden-Layer Neural Network (nnet)

Theory. A feedforward network with one hidden layer of \(H\) units computes a composition of linear maps and pointwise nonlinearities:

\[ \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}) = g_o\!\left( \boldsymbol{\beta}_0 + \sum_{h=1}^H \beta_h \cdot g_h\!\left( \alpha_{h0} + \sum_{j=1}^p \alpha_{hj} x_j \right) \right) \]

The hidden-unit activation \(g_h\) is typically the logistic sigmoid \(g_h(a) = (1+e^{-a})^{-1}\); the output activation \(g_o\) is the identity for regression and softmax for classification. By the universal approximation theorem (Hornik, Stinchcombe, and White 1989), a single hidden layer with sufficiently many units can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain — but this result is existential, not constructive.15

Parameters are estimated by minimising a weight-decay-regularised loss: \[ L_{\text{reg}} = L(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\!\left(\sum_{h,j}\alpha_{hj}^2 + \sum_h\beta_h^2\right) \] using backpropagation (Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams 1986) and the BFGS quasi-Newton optimiser implemented in nnet.

Key hyperparameters: size (hidden units \(H\)), decay (weight regularisation \(\lambda\)), maxit (maximum iterations).

fit_nnet <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "nnet",
                spec = list(size = 5, decay = 0.01, linout = TRUE,
                            trace = FALSE))
fit_nnet
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: nnet
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.11 Ensemble Aggregation

The stacking and SuperLearner methods combine multiple base learners into a single ensemble. Unlike bagging (which averages homogeneous learners) and boosting (which combines sequentially), these methods learn an optimal combination of heterogeneous learners.

5.11.1 Stacking (stacking)

Theory. Stacked generalisation (Wolpert 1992; Breiman 1996b) uses a meta-learner to combine out-of-fold predictions from a set of diverse base learners. Let \(\hat{f}_1, \ldots, \hat{f}_L\) be \(L\) base learners. For each observation \(i\), collect cross-validated predictions from each base learner into a meta-feature matrix:

\[ \tilde{\mathbf{X}} =\begin{pmatrix} \hat{f}_1^{(-1)}(\mathbf{x}_1) & \cdots &\hat{f}_L^{(-1)}(\mathbf{x}_1)\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \hat{f}_1^{(-n)}(\mathbf{x}_n) & \cdots &\hat{f}_L^{(-n)}(\mathbf{x}_n) \end{pmatrix} \]

where the superscript \((-i)\) indicates that observation \(i\) was excluded from the training fold. A meta-learner (default: GLM in funcml) is trained on \(\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\) to produce the final prediction. The use of out-of-fold predictions prevents the meta-learner from over-weighting base learners that memorised the training data.16

Key hyperparameters: learners (base learner IDs), meta_learner (default "glm").

fit_stack <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "stacking",
                 spec = list(learners = c("glm", "rpart", "ranger"),
                             meta_learner = "glm"))
fit_stack
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: stacking
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

5.11.2 SuperLearner (superlearner)

Theory. The SuperLearner (Laan, Polley, and Hubbard 2007; Polley and Laan 2010) selects the optimal convex combination of base learner cross-validated predictions:

\[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha} \ge \mathbf{0},\; \mathbf{1}^\top\boldsymbol{\alpha} = 1} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n L\!\left(y_i,\; \sum_{l=1}^L \alpha_l\, \hat{f}_l^{(-i)}(\mathbf{x}_i)\right) \]

The convex hull constraint (\(\alpha_l \ge 0\), \(\sum_l \alpha_l = 1\)) ensures the ensemble never extrapolates beyond the support of its base learners. The SuperLearner is asymptotically optimal: under mild conditions, it converges to the oracle-best convex combination of the candidate learners, and if one of the candidates is the true model, the SuperLearner will converge to it (Laan, Polley, and Hubbard 2007).

The difference between stacking and SuperLearner is therefore the constraint. SuperLearner is conservative (never worse than the best base learner asymptotically); stacking’s unconstrained meta-learner can outperform any individual candidate but may also overfit.

fit_sl <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "superlearner",
              spec = list(learners = c("glm", "rpart", "ranger")))
fit_sl
#> <funcml_fit> regression model: superlearner
#> Formula: birth_weight_g ~ age + lwt + race + smoke + ptl + ht + ui + ftv
#> Features: 8 | Obs: 189

The learner registry provides the models; the next section provides the vocabulary for quantifying their quality.

6 Performance Metrics

funcml exposes 18 metrics organised into four families. All share the same call signature: metric(truth, pred) or metric(truth, prob_matrix) for probability-based measures.

6.1 Regression Metrics

Let \(\{(y_i, \hat{y}_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) be truth–prediction pairs and \(\bar{y} = n^{-1}\sum_i y_i\).

6.2 Classification Metrics

For binary classification with \(y \in \{0, 1\}\), let TP, FP, FN, TN denote confusion matrix counts.

6.3 Probabilistic Metrics

These metrics require predicted probability outputs (type = "prob") and measure the quality of the full probability distribution, not just the predicted class.

Log-loss (cross-entropy) penalises confident wrong predictions more than uncertain ones: \[ \mathcal{L}_{\log} = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K y_{ik}\log\hat{p}_{ik} \]

Brier score (Brier 1950) measures mean-squared probability error, decomposable into resolution, reliability, and uncertainty: \[ \text{BS} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K (\hat{p}_{ik} - y_{ik})^2 \]

AUC (Fawcett 2006) is the area under the ROC curve — equal to the probability that a randomly chosen positive observation receives a higher predicted score than a randomly chosen negative observation. For multiclass problems, the Hand–Till (Hand and Till 2001) extension averages pairwise AUC values.17

6.4 Calibration Metrics

A model is calibrated if \(\hat{P}(Y = 1 \mid \hat{p} = p) \approx p\) for all \(p\). Among observations with predicted probability near 0.7, for instance, roughly 70% should actually be positive. Calibration is distinct from discrimination: a model can rank patients correctly (high AUC) but systematically overestimate risk (poor calibration).

Let \(\{B_m\}_{m=1}^M\) partition the predicted probability range. The Expected Calibration Error (ECE) is the weighted average absolute gap between accuracy and confidence across bins: \[ \text{ECE} = \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{|B_m|}{n} \bigl|\text{acc}(B_m) - \text{conf}(B_m)\bigr| \]

The Maximum Calibration Error (MCE) is the worst-case gap: \[ \text{MCE} = \max_m \bigl|\text{acc}(B_m) - \text{conf}(B_m)\bigr| \]

truth <- data_reg$birth_weight_g
pred  <- predict(fit_ranger, newdata = data_reg)

rmse(truth, pred)
#> [1] 397.7631
mae(truth, pred)
#> [1] 318.373
rsq(truth, pred)
#> [1] 0.700882

Metrics only carry meaning when computed on held-out data. The next section shows how evaluate() handles this automatically via cross-validation.

7 Resampling-Based Evaluation

The evaluate() function performs \(K\)-fold cross-validated model assessment and returns a funcml_eval object with fold-level results, summary statistics, and confidence intervals.

eval_reg <- evaluate(
  data       = data_reg,
  formula    = formula_reg,
  model      = "ranger",
  resampling = cv(v = 5, seed = 42),
  metrics    = c("rmse", "mae", "rsq"),
  seed       = 42
)
eval_reg
#> <funcml_eval> model: ranger | task: regression
#>   metric         mean         sd n   std_error conf_level     conf_low

#> 2    mae 539.74832513 50.7930993 5 22.71536457       0.95 476.68036235
#> 3    rsq   0.08947187  0.1109587 5  0.04962222       0.95  -0.04830151
#>     conf_high
#> 1 734.3373366
#> 2 602.8162879
#> 3   0.2272453
eval_cls <- evaluate(
  data       = data_cls,
  formula    = formula_cls,
  model      = "ranger",
  resampling = cv(v = 5, seed = 42),
  metrics    = c("accuracy", "auc", "logloss"),
  type       = "prob",
  seed       = 42
)
eval_cls
#> <funcml_eval> model: ranger | task: classification
#>     metric      mean         sd n  std_error conf_level  conf_low conf_high
#> 1 accuracy 0.7356254 0.06873875 5 0.03074090       0.95 0.6502750 0.8209758
#> 2      auc 0.8151028 0.07572365 5 0.03386464       0.95 0.7210795 0.9091262
#> 3  logloss 0.5011082 0.08653768 5 0.03870083       0.95 0.3936574 0.6085589

The plot() method displays the fold-level metric distribution, providing a visual sense of estimator variance across folds:

plot(eval_reg)

Cross-validation gives a performance estimate for fixed hyperparameters. The next section shows how to search for configurations that improve on these defaults.

8 Hyperparameter Tuning

8.1 Theory

Most learners have hyperparameters — configuration choices made before training — that substantially affect generalisation performance. Let \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} \in \Lambda\) be the hyperparameter vector. The tuning objective is:

\[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\lambda} \in \Lambda} \widehat{\text{CV}}_K(f_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}) \]

Grid search exhaustively evaluates all combinations in a user-specified grid \(\{\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{(g)}\}_{g=1}^G\). It scales exponentially with the number of hyperparameters but is deterministic and interpretable.

Random search (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009) samples \(N_{\text{eval}}\) configurations uniformly at random from \(\Lambda\). In high-dimensional hyperparameter spaces it is usually more efficient than grid search because it avoids wasting evaluations on redundant dimensions — if one hyperparameter matters far more than others, random search spreads evaluations across that dimension more broadly than a regular grid.

Nested cross-validation produces an unbiased estimate of the generalisation error of the entire model-selection pipeline by wrapping the inner tuning loop in an outer evaluation loop:

\[ \text{Err}_{\text{tuned}} = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \widehat{\text{CV}}_K^{\text{outer}}\!\!\left( \hat{f}_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}(\mathcal{D}^{\text{train}})} \right) \right] \]

WarningModel selection bias

Evaluating a tuned model on the same data used for tuning produces an optimistically biased performance estimate. The selected \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\) is the configuration that happened to perform best on that particular resample, not necessarily the best for new data. Nested CV corrects this by evaluating the entire tuning procedure — selection included — on held-out outer folds.

8.2 Grid and Random Search

grid_rpart <- expand.grid(
  cp       = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05),
  minsplit = c(5, 10, 20)
)

tune_rpart <- tune(
  data       = data_reg,
  formula    = formula_reg,
  model      = "rpart",
  grid       = grid_rpart,
  resampling = cv(v = 5, seed = 42),
  metric     = "rmse",
  search     = "grid",
  seed       = 42
)

tune_rpart
#> <funcml_tune> metric=rmse direction=min search=grid
#> Best:
#>     cp minsplit     mean       sd n std_error conf_level conf_low conf_high
#> 8 0.01       20 668.7932 48.72219 5  21.78923       0.95 608.2967  729.2898
tune_rpart$best
#>     cp minsplit     mean       sd n std_error conf_level conf_low conf_high
#> 8 0.01       20 668.7932 48.72219 5  21.78923       0.95 608.2967  729.2898
grid_ranger <- expand.grid(
  num.trees = c(100, 200, 300),
  mtry      = c(2, 3, 5)
)

tune_ranger <- tune(
  data       = data_reg,
  formula    = formula_reg,
  model      = "ranger",
  grid       = grid_ranger,
  resampling = cv(v = 5, seed = 42),
  metric     = "rmse",
  search     = "random",
  n_evals    = 6,
  seed       = 42
)

tune_ranger$best
#>   num.trees mtry    mean       sd n std_error conf_level conf_low conf_high
#> 5       200    2 675.227 48.80216 5  21.82499       0.95 614.6311  735.8228
plot(tune_rpart)

8.3 Nested Cross-Validation

nested <- tune(
  data             = data_reg,
  formula          = formula_reg,
  model            = "rpart",
  grid             = grid_rpart,
  resampling       = cv(v = 3, seed = 1),
  outer_resampling = cv(v = 4, seed = 2),
  metric           = "rmse",
  seed             = 42
)
nested

With hyperparameters selected, the natural next step is to see whether the chosen learner is competitive with alternatives on the same task.

9 Learner Comparison

The compare_learners() function benchmarks multiple learners under a shared resampling design and metric set. All learners see the same folds, making the comparison fair and the results directly comparable.18

cmp <- compare_learners(
  data       = data_reg,
  formula    = formula_reg,
  models     = c("glm", "rpart", "ranger", "gbm", "xgboost"),
  resampling = cv(v = 5, seed = 42),
  metrics    = c("rmse", "mae"),
  seed       = 42
)
cmp

TipHow to read a benchmark

A GLM baseline is essential. If a complex model (boosting, random forest) cannot beat the linear baseline by a meaningful margin, the added complexity is not justified. Conversely, a large gap suggests substantial non-linearity or interactions in the data. RMSE differences should be compared relative to the outcome’s standard deviation: a 50-gram RMSE improvement on a 750-gram outcome SD is meaningful; a 2-gram improvement is noise.

Having identified a performant learner, the next question is not merely how well it performs, but why — which features drive the predictions and how. That is the focus of the interpretation section.

10 Model Interpretation

10.1 Overview

The interpret() function provides a unified gateway to fourteen model-agnostic interpretation methods, all operating on a funcml_fit object and a reference dataset. The methods fall into three groups by scope:

Scope Methods
Global (population-level) VIP, Permutation, PDP, ALE, Interaction, Surrogate
Local (individual prediction) ICE, LIME, Local model, SHAP, Ceteris paribus
Diagnostic Calibration

All methods return a structured S3 object with print(), summary(), and plot() methods. We use a Random Forest on the birthweight data as the black-box model throughout.

fit_rf_reg <- fit(formula_reg, data = data_reg, model = "ranger",
                  spec = list(num.trees = 300, seed = 42))

10.2 Variable Importance (Model-Based VIP)

Theory. Many models expose a native importance measure derived from their internal structure. For tree ensembles, the mean-decrease impurity (MDI) sums the weighted impurity reduction at all nodes where feature \(j\) was used, across all trees in the ensemble:

\[ \text{VIP}(j) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}^{(b)}_j} \frac{n_t}{n}\,\Delta\text{Impurity}(t) \]

For linear models, importance is derived from standardised absolute coefficients. The vip method automatically dispatches to the model’s native mechanism when available; otherwise it falls back to permutation importance (B. Greenwell and Boehmke 2020).

WarningLimitation of MDI importance

MDI is biased toward features with many unique values (continuous variables, high-cardinality factors) and toward features used early in trees. When features are correlated, MDI inflates the importance of correlated groups (Strobl et al. 2007). For unbiased importance estimates, prefer permutation importance (Section 10.2) or conditional permutation importance from cforest.

vip_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "vip")
plot(vip_obj)

10.3 Permutation Importance

Theory. Permutation-based importance (A. Fisher, Rudin, and Dominici 2019; Breiman 2001b) measures the predictive value of each feature by breaking its association with the response. For each feature \(j\), the values of \(x_j\) across the dataset are randomly permuted, the model is re-applied without retraining, and the increase in prediction error is recorded:

\[ \text{PI}(j) = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \hat{L}_s(\pi_j) - \hat{L} \]

where \(\hat{L}\) is the baseline loss on the original data, \(\hat{L}_s(\pi_j)\) the loss after permuting feature \(j\) in repetition \(s\), and \(S\) the number of permutation repetitions. A large increase signals that the feature was genuinely useful; a small increase (near zero) means the model’s predictions were insensitive to that feature.

Permutation importance is model-agnostic — it treats the model as a black box — and is linked directly to the chosen evaluation metric.19 The ratio version \(\text{PI}_{\text{ratio}}(j) = \hat{L}(\pi_j)/\hat{L}\) is scale-independent and useful for comparing across datasets.

perm_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "permute",
                      metric = "rmse", nsim = 20, seed = 42)
plot(perm_obj)

10.4 Partial Dependence Plots (PDP)

Theory. The partial dependence function for feature \(j\) (J. H. Friedman 2001b; B. M. Greenwell 2017) shows the average model prediction as \(x_j\) varies, marginalising over the joint distribution of all other features:

\[ \hat{f}_j(z) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{-j}}\!\left[\hat{f}(z, \mathbf{x}_{-j})\right] \approx \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{f}(z, x_{i,-j}) \]

This Monte Carlo approximation substitutes the observed values of all other features for the complement \(\mathbf{x}_{-j}\). The PDP shows the marginal population-level effect of \(x_j\): if \(x_j\) were changed to value \(z\) for every observation, what would the average prediction be?

WarningPDP and correlated features

The PDP averages over the observed marginal distribution of \(\mathbf{x}_{-j}\), which can include combinations \((z, \mathbf{x}_{-j})\) that never occur in the data when features are correlated. For example, if height and weight are strongly correlated, a PDP might average predictions for (height = 200cm, weight = 40kg) — a biologically impossible combination. ALE plots (Section 10.6) resolve this by conditioning on local neighbourhoods rather than the global marginal.

pdp_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "pdp",
                     features = "lwt")
plot(pdp_obj)

10.5 Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE)

Theory. ICE curves (Goldstein et al. 2015) disaggregate the PDP: instead of averaging, we display the prediction profile for each individual observation as \(x_j\) varies:

\[ \hat{f}_j^{(i)}(z) = \hat{f}(z, \mathbf{x}_{i,-j}), \quad i = 1, \ldots, n \]

Each line shows what would happen to one specific observation’s prediction if only \(x_j\) were changed. The PDP is the vertical mean of all ICE curves.

The diagnostic power of ICE lies in heterogeneity. If all ICE lines are parallel and non-crossing, the effect of \(x_j\) is the same for everyone and there are no interactions involving \(x_j\). If lines cross or have different slopes, the effect of \(x_j\) depends on the values of other features — there is an interaction.20

ice_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "ice",
                     features = "lwt")
plot(ice_obj)

10.6 Accumulated Local Effects (ALE)

Theory. Accumulated local effects (Apley and Zhu 2020) address the extrapolation problem of PDP by conditioning on local neighbourhoods of \(x_j\) rather than integrating over the global marginal. The main effect ALE for feature \(j\) at value \(z\) is defined as:

\[ \hat{f}_j^{\text{ALE}}(z) = \int_{z_0}^z \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \frac{\partial\hat{f}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial x_j} \;\bigg|\; x_j = t \right] dt \;-\; C \]

where \(C\) is a centering constant ensuring zero mean. In practice, the interval \([z_0, z]\) is discretised into \(K\) bins \([z_{k-1}, z_k]\) and the integral replaced by accumulated finite differences:

\[ \hat{f}_j^{\text{ALE}}(z_K) \approx \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{1}{|N_k|} \sum_{i:\, x_{ij} \in [z_{k-1}, z_k]} \!\!\bigl[\hat{f}(z_k, \mathbf{x}_{i,-j}) - \hat{f}(z_{k-1}, \mathbf{x}_{i,-j})\bigr] \]

where \(N_k = \{i : x_{ij} \in [z_{k-1}, z_k]\}\) is the set of observations falling in bin \(k\). Because the differences are computed only for observations whose \(x_j\) lies within each bin, the method never evaluates the model at combinations that cannot arise given the observed data distribution, even under strong feature correlation.21

ale_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "ale",
                     features = "lwt")
plot(ale_obj)

10.7 LIME — Local Surrogate Explanations

Theory. LIME (Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin 2016) explains a single prediction \(\hat{f}(\mathbf{x}^*)\) by fitting a simple, interpretable surrogate model \(g\) in a neighbourhood of \(\mathbf{x}^*\):

\[ \hat{g} = \arg\min_{g \in \mathcal{G}}\, \mathcal{L}(\hat{f}, g, \pi_{\mathbf{x}^*}) + \Omega(g) \]

where \(\mathcal{G}\) is a class of interpretable models (sparse linear models or decision trees), \(\pi_{\mathbf{x}^*}(\mathbf{x}) = \exp(-d(\mathbf{x}^*, \mathbf{x})^2/\sigma^2)\) is a locality kernel weighting samples by proximity to \(\mathbf{x}^*\), \(\mathcal{L}\) is a weighted fidelity loss measuring how well \(g\) approximates \(\hat{f}\) near \(\mathbf{x}^*\), and \(\Omega(g)\) penalises model complexity.

In funcml, LIME uses a local weighted linear regression where weights are derived from Gower distance — a distance metric that handles mixed-type features by normalising each variable to \([0,1]\) and using the absolute difference for continuous variables and a 0/1 indicator for categorical variables.

The key idea is that while \(\hat{f}\) may be globally non-linear and complex, it is often locally linear in a small neighbourhood around any query point. The local linear model \(\hat{g}\) is the tangent-plane approximation of \(\hat{f}\) at \(\mathbf{x}^*\).

lime_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "lime",
                      newdata = data_reg[5, , drop = FALSE],
                      k = 3, seed = 42)
plot(lime_obj)

10.8 Local Surrogate Models (IML-style)

Theory. The local_model method constructs an explicit local neighbourhood by finding the \(k\) nearest training observations to \(\mathbf{x}^*\) under Gower distance and fitting a weighted lasso (sparse linear model) on this neighbourhood. The Gower distance between \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{x}'\) is:

\[ d_{\text{Gower}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \frac{1}{p}\sum_{j=1}^p \delta_j(x_j, x_j') \]

where \(\delta_j\) is a feature-type-appropriate dissimilarity: the absolute range-normalised difference \(|x_j - x_j'|/r_j\) for continuous features, and the 0/1 mismatch indicator for nominal features. The local lasso fit provides sparse feature attributions: coefficients are interpretable as the local marginal effect of each feature on the model’s prediction near \(\mathbf{x}^*\).

The difference between lime and local_model in funcml is subtle: lime perturbs \(\mathbf{x}^*\) to generate a neighbourhood; local_model uses the \(k\) nearest training observations. The former is better when the training distribution is sparse; the latter is more stable when training data is dense.

local_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "local_model",
                       newdata = data_reg[5, , drop = FALSE],
                       k = 10, seed = 42)
plot(local_obj)

10.9 SHAP Attributions

Theory. Shapley values (Shapley 1953) originate in cooperative game theory. Consider a prediction as a game where features are players that cooperate to produce the model output. The Shapley value of player \(j\) is its fair share of the total payout — the average marginal contribution of feature \(j\) across all possible orderings in which features could have joined the coalition:

\[ \phi_j(\hat{f}, \mathbf{x}) = \sum_{S \subseteq \mathcal{F} \setminus \{j\}} \frac{|S|!\,(p-|S|-1)!}{p!} \left[ v(S \cup \{j\}) - v(S) \right] \]

where \(v(S)\) is the model output when only features in \(S\) are known and others are integrated out (typically using the training-data marginal). Intuitively: for each possible subset \(S\) not including \(j\), we measure how much adding \(j\) improves the prediction, and average over all possible subset orders weighted by their probability.

SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017) provides efficient approximations to these Shapley values and guarantees three axiomatic properties:

  • Local accuracy: the sum of all SHAP values equals the difference between the prediction and the baseline \(\hat{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \phi_0 + \sum_j \phi_j(\mathbf{x})\).
  • Missingness: features with no effect on any prediction receive \(\phi_j = 0\).
  • Consistency: if a model changes so that feature \(j\)’s marginal contribution never decreases, its Shapley value cannot decrease.

For tree ensembles, exact Shapley values can be computed in \(O(TLD^2)\) time (Lundberg et al. 2020), where \(T\) is the number of trees, \(L\) the maximum leaves, and \(D\) the maximum depth.22

The shap method returns a shapviz object that supports a range of visualisation types through the kind argument.

shap_local <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "shap",
                        newdata = data_reg[5, , drop = FALSE],
                        nsim = 50, seed = 42)
plot(shap_local, kind = "waterfall")

For a global view, compute SHAP values for all observations and aggregate:

shap_all <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "shap",
                      newdata = data_reg,
                      nsim = 50, seed = 42)
plot(shap_all, kind = "beeswarm")
plot(shap_all, kind = "bar")
NoteSHAP vs. permutation importance vs. LIME

Permutation importance is global and model-agnostic but does not explain individual predictions. LIME explains individual predictions but is unstable — small changes in the neighbourhood or the perturbation distribution can change explanations substantially. SHAP is both locally accurate and globally consistent: individual SHAP values sum to the prediction (local accuracy), and aggregated over all observations they recover a global importance ranking (mean |SHAP|). For most applications, SHAP is preferable when computation allows; permutation importance is a fast, interpretable alternative for global ranking; LIME is most useful when a simple human-readable explanation is needed for a single prediction.

10.10 Global Surrogate Trees

Theory. A global surrogate approximates the full black-box model with a single interpretable model trained on its predictions (Molnar, Casalicchio, and Bischl 2018). A decision tree is the standard choice:

\[ \hat{g} = \arg\min_{g \in \text{Trees}} \sum_{i=1}^n L\!\bigl(\hat{f}(\mathbf{x}_i),\, g(\mathbf{x}_i)\bigr) \]

The fidelity of the approximation is measured by the \(R^2\) between \(\hat{g}\) and \(\hat{f}\). A high-fidelity surrogate provides a global, rule-based explanation of the black box. A low-fidelity surrogate means the tree is too simple to capture the model’s logic, and any rules extracted from it are misleading.23

surr_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "surrogate",
                      spec = list(cp = 0.01))
plot(surr_obj)

10.11 Feature Interaction Strength

Theory. The H-statistic (J. H. Friedman and Popescu 2008) quantifies the proportion of a feature pair’s joint effect that is not explained by the sum of their individual main effects — a formal interaction measure derived from partial dependence functions:

\[ H_{jk}^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \bigl[ \hat{f}_{jk}(x_{ij}, x_{ik}) - \hat{f}_j(x_{ij}) - \hat{f}_k(x_{ik}) \bigr]^2} {\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{f}_{jk}^2(x_{ij}, x_{ik})} \]

\(H_{jk} = 0\) indicates that the joint effect is fully decomposable into main effects (no interaction); \(H_{jk} = 1\) indicates that the entire joint effect is due to interaction with no main-effect components.

The total interaction strength of feature \(j\) with all other features is the complement of the main-effect proportion: \[ H_j^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i \hat{f}_j^2(x_{ij})}{\sum_i \hat{f}^2(\mathbf{x}_i)} \]

int_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg, method = "interaction")
plot(int_obj)

10.12 Ceteris Paribus Profiles

Theory. A ceteris-paribus (CP) profile — also called a prediction profile or what-if curve — traces the prediction for a specific observation as one feature is varied while all others are held at their observed values:

\[ h_j^{(i)}(z) = \hat{f}(x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{i,j-1},\; z,\; x_{i,j+1}, \ldots, x_{ip}) \]

This is identical to an ICE curve for observation \(i\); the difference is interpretive. ICE plots compare heterogeneity across many observations; CP profiles are used for counterfactual analysis of a single case: “what would happen to this patient’s predicted risk if their glucose level were 50 points lower?”

cp_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_reg, data_reg,
                    method  = "ceteris_paribus",
                    newdata = data_reg[5, , drop = FALSE],
                    features = c("lwt", "age", "smoke"))
plot(cp_obj)

10.13 Calibration Analysis

Theory. Probability calibration (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005) assesses whether predicted probabilities are numerically faithful to empirical frequencies. The reliability diagram bins predictions into \(M\) equal- frequency intervals and plots \((\text{mean predicted prob.}, \text{observed fraction})\) for each bin. Perfect calibration falls on the diagonal.

NoteCalibration vs. discrimination

A model can have excellent AUC (it ranks patients correctly) but be severely miscalibrated (it assigns systematically wrong probabilities). Conversely, a well-calibrated model may have mediocre AUC. For risk communication and decision support, both properties matter: discrimination determines whether the model distinguishes cases from controls; calibration determines whether the stated probability is trustworthy as a number (e.g., “this patient has a 78% predicted risk”).

fit_rf_cls <- fit(formula_cls, data = data_cls, model = "ranger",
                  spec = list(num.trees = 300, seed = 42))

cal_obj <- interpret(fit_rf_cls, data_cls, method = "calibration",
                     type = "prob", pos_level = "Yes", bins = 10)
plot(cal_obj, style = "curve")

With a comprehensive interpretation of the selected model in hand, we can move from prediction to causal inference — asking not just what the model predicts, but what would happen if we intervened on a treatment variable.

11 Plug-In G-Computation

11.1 Theory

G-computation (Robins 1986; Snowden, Rose, and Mortimer 2011) is a standardisation-based plug-in estimator of the g-formula (Robins’ generalised formula). Under three identifiability assumptions — consistency (\(Y_i^a = Y_i\) when \(A_i = a\)), conditional exchangeability (\(Y^a \perp\!\!\!\perp A \mid \mathbf{X}\), no unmeasured confounding), and positivity (\(P(A = a \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}) > 0\) for all \(\mathbf{x}\) in the support) — the potential-outcome mean under treatment \(a\) is identified as (Pearl 2009; Snowden, Rose, and Mortimer 2011):

\[ \psi^a = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\!\bigl[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid A = a, \mathbf{X}]\bigr] = \int \mathbb{E}[Y \mid A = a, \mathbf{x}]\;dP(\mathbf{x}) \]

The plug-in estimator replaces \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid A, \mathbf{X}]\) with a fitted regression model \(\hat{f}\) and standardises over the empirical covariate distribution:

\[ \hat{\psi}^a = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{f}(a, \mathbf{x}_i) \]

Four estimands are supported:

Estimand Formula Population
ATE \(\hat{\psi}^1 - \hat{\psi}^0\) All observations
ATT \(n_1^{-1}\sum_{i: A_i=1}[\hat{f}(1,\mathbf{x}_i) - \hat{f}(0,\mathbf{x}_i)]\) Treated only
CATE \(\hat{f}(1,\mathbf{x}) - \hat{f}(0,\mathbf{x})\) As a function of \(\mathbf{x}\)
IATE CATE evaluated at each observed \(\mathbf{x}_i\) Individualised

Uncertainty is quantified via normal approximation or bootstrap resampling. The use of flexible machine learning models for \(\hat{f}\) relaxes parametric assumptions on the outcome surface.

ImportantCausal assumptions are not software guarantees

G-computation produces a causal estimate only when the three identifiability assumptions hold. The software cannot verify conditional exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding) — this is a substantive, domain-specific judgment. Similarly, the plug-in estimator can be biased if the outcome model is misspecified. Doubly robust estimators (e.g., augmented IPW, TMLE) can provide some protection against outcome-model misspecification but are outside the current scope of funcml.

11.2 R Code

data_causal       <- data_reg
data_causal$smoke <- factor(data_causal$smoke,
                            levels = c(0, 1),
                            labels = c("non_smoker", "smoker"))
ate_obj <- estimate(
  data      = data_causal,
  formula   = birth_weight_g ~ smoke + age + lwt + race + ptl + ht + ui + ftv,
  model     = "ranger",
  treatment = "smoke",
  estimand  = "ATE",
  interval  = "bootstrap",
  n_boot    = 200,
  seed      = 42
)
ate_obj
#> <funcml_estimand> ATE via g-computation
#> Treatment: smoke (smoker vs non_smoker)
#> Estimate: -171.5528 | SE: 14.8517 | 95% bootstrap CI [-332.8115, -70.6763]
att_obj <- estimate(
  data      = data_causal,
  formula   = birth_weight_g ~ smoke + age + lwt + race + ptl + ht + ui + ftv,
  model     = "ranger",
  treatment = "smoke",
  estimand  = "ATT",
  interval  = "bootstrap",
  n_boot    = 200,
  seed      = 42
)
att_obj
#> <funcml_estimand> ATT via g-computation
#> Treatment: smoke (smoker vs non_smoker)
#> Estimate: -190.8182 | SE: 20.5053 | 95% bootstrap CI [-341.7107, -69.7277]
cate_obj <- estimate(
  data      = data_causal,
  formula   = birth_weight_g ~ smoke + age + lwt + race + ptl + ht + ui + ftv,
  model     = "ranger",
  treatment = "smoke",
  estimand  = "CATE",
  newdata   = data_causal,
  seed      = 42
)
head(cate_obj$estimates)
#> NULL

The preceding sections have introduced each component of the framework in isolation. The next section brings them together in a single, coherent analysis.

12 End-to-End Workflow

This section demonstrates a complete analysis of the Pima diabetes dataset, proceeding through every stage of the funcml workflow in sequence: baseline benchmarking, tuning, interpretation, and calibration.

12.1 Step 1: Baseline Benchmark

We begin by comparing five learners under the same 5-fold CV design and three complementary metrics — accuracy, AUC, and log-loss. No hyperparameter tuning is applied at this stage; we use defaults.

cmp_cls <- compare_learners(
  data       = data_cls,
  formula    = formula_cls,
  models     = c("glm", "rpart", "ranger", "gbm", "xgboost"),
  resampling = cv(v = 5, seed = 42),
  metrics    = c("accuracy", "auc", "logloss"),
  type       = "prob",
  seed       = 42
)
cmp_cls
